newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan seen posting first deficit in six years.
newsitem.headline: Japan seen posting first deficit in six years.

text.p: Special factors will likely cause Japan to post its first current account trade deficit in six years when it releases figures for January, economists say.
But a surplus is expected to resume soon and threatens to become a source of trade friction.

In a Reuters poll the average of economists' forecasts was for the January figures to show a deficit of 31 billion yen ($258 million) in the current account, the broadest measure of merchandise and services trade, compared with a surplus of 32.6 billion yen ($272 million) a year earlier.
Economists said the data, to be announced on Thursday, would be exaggerated by seasonal factors.
January figures are notoriously unpredictable as the length of the New Year Holiday, including weekends, varies from year to year, affecting the number of business days.

Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus for January, which was announced last month, dropped a hefty 91.7 percent from a year earlier. But the closely watched surplus with the United States rose 81.6 percent in January.
Economists said the balance of payments is most likely to be in surplus in February, and to start showing a year-on-year rise in the near future.

"The surplus (on an unadjusted basis) will be rising by the second quarter of this year... If we see the surplus rising sharply, that could lead to trade friction," said Peter Morgan, an economist at HSBC James Capel Japan.
He said the current account surplus may have hit a floor in April last year on a seasonally adjusted basis.

Japan's contentious current account surplus fell for the 16th consecutive month of year-on-year declines in December. But the pace of the falls has slowed due the the yen's drop since mid-1995, which has boosted exports while discouraging imports.
The United States is now warning Japan against a rise in its trade surplus.

"Too often in the past we have seen cycles in which Japan's trade surplus has declined with consequent reductions in trade frictions only to rise again," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Friday.
He said the United States will continue to press Japan to open up its markets, with America's focus on ensuring that Tokyo lives up to past trade agreements.
Officials at Japan's Finance Ministry have been saying that Japan's current account surplus is on a declining trend as the rise in imports has been larger than that of exports.

But economists said a planned increase in Japan's consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1 could slow domestic consumption and in turn encourage Japanese firms to step up exports to retain overall profits.
Prices of crude oil imports, which have been a major factor pushing up Japan's overall import costs, are not expected to serve as a leading booster for overall imports any longer, economists said.
Crude oil prices, which kept rising last year, causing a hefty rise in overall imports, have been falling since the beginning of this year.
